content.text:
Confirmed the review ran against the right thing — PR #1741 (`fix/hermes-python-interpreter` → `main`) touches exactly the three files reviewed.

## Findings

**1. Broken endpoint scheme — `ansible/roles/ai-dev/defaults/main.yaml:13`** (medium, the only one I'd call blocking)

`ai_dev_hermes_docker_host: tcp://docker-host:2375` is still written into `~/.config/hermes/env` (`hermes.yaml:120`), but the Docker CLI — the only thing that understood the `tcp://` scheme — is what this PR removes. The docs now say the agent queries the proxy directly over HTTP, and `curl "$DOCKER_HOST/containers/json"` fails with "unsupported protocol". The proxy's own healthcheck in `docker/init/compose.yml:101` already uses `http://…:2375`. Either change the value to `http://docker-host:2375` or export a separate HTTP-scheme variable; as shipped, the one endpoint the agent is meant to use is spelled in a form nothing left on the host can consume.

**2. Mask removal without a daemon-reload — `ansible/roles/ai-dev/tasks/hermes.yaml:83`** (low)

"Remove masks for the departed Docker units" deletes `/etc/systemd/system/docker.{service,socket}` with no `systemctl daemon-reload` (no handler, no follow-up command). systemd holds the mask in in-memory unit state until a reload or reboot, so on the migrating run `systemctl is-enabled docker.service` still reports `masked` and anything querying unit state before the next reboot sees stale data.

**3. Unscoped package removal + weak assert — `ansible/roles/ai-dev/tasks/hermes.yaml:76`** (low)

`containerd`, `runc`, and `libpathrs` go to `pacman --remove` with no dependency handling. These are shared runtimes, not the client: if anything else depends on one — now or after a future package addition — `pacman -R` fails on dependency break and the play aborts, and then the permanent assert at line 198 fails on every subsequent run even though the host genuinely can't launch containers. Worth scoping the hard assert to `docker`/`containerd` and treating the transitive libs as best-effort. Related but not a bug: the assert matches exact names only, so `docker-bin`, `podman`, `crun`, or `lxc` would pass it despite the fail_msg's "must never be able to run containers" claim.

## What's fine

The new assert's Jinja is correct (`select('in', list)` applies `item in list`, and filter binding beats `==`), and the interpreter pin lands on both — and only — the `become_user: hermes` tasks, which is the right scope.
resolve each of these and commit changes to the existing PR

through its bundled browser, and container logs, which are strings written by
whatever produced them. It therefore runs as its own `hermes` account, not as
the management user. `/home/michael` is mode `0750`, so the agent cannot read
the management user's GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or Claude and Codex sessions.
That separation is the point: scoping the agent's own credentials achieves
nothing while broader credentials sit beside it in the same home directory.

Ansible owns the account, installs the agent with `--skip-setup`, and deploys
its credentials. The installer clones `NousResearch/hermes-agent` into
`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, builds a uv virtualenv, links `~/.local/bin/hermes`,
and pulls a Hermes-managed Node and a Playwright browser, so the first run is
long and the install is the largest on the VM.

ai-dev carries no Docker client. The socket proxy speaks plain HTTP, so the
agent queries it directly, and `DOCKER_HOST` records the endpoint. Installing
the client would drag in `containerd` and `runc`, about 100 MiB of container
runtime on the one guest that must never run containers; masking the daemon
afterwards only suppresses that, since a mask is one `systemctl unmask` away
from being undone. The role therefore asserts those packages stay absent.
The trade-off is `GET /containers/{id}/logs`, which returns a multiplexed
stream the CLI would otherwise de-multiplex.

### Access tiers

The agent observes broadly, acts narrowly, and proposes everything else.

| Tier | Reach | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observe | Proxmox cluster and guest state | `PVEAuditor` API token |
| Observe | Containers, logs, stats, events | Read-only socket proxy |
| Propose | Any change to this repository | GitHub token, pull request only |

content.text:
All three findings are fixed and pushed to PR #1741 as `d08c1819`.

**1. Endpoint scheme** — `ai_dev_hermes_docker_host` is now `http://docker-host:2375`, matching what the proxy actually serves (its own healthcheck in `docker/init/compose.yml:101` uses the same scheme). Nothing left on the host can parse `tcp://`.

**2. Stale mask state** — the mask-removal task now `notify`s a new `reload systemd units` handler in `ansible/roles/ai-dev/handlers/main.yaml`, so systemd drops the in-memory mask on the migrating run instead of at the next boot. I used a handler rather than an inline `when: ... is changed` task because the role already has a handlers file and the inline form trips ansible-lint's `no-handler`.

**3. Package list** — rather than splitting into hard-required and best-effort removals, I removed the cause of the dependency break: `libpathrs` is gone from the list. It's a path-resolution library that pacman itself depends on, and it can't launch a container on its own, so listing it risked aborting the play (and breaking the package manager) for no security gain. The remaining entries are all true runtimes with no other dependents once Docker is gone, so a single hard-asserted list still works. I also widened it to `crun`, `docker-bin`, `lxc`, and `podman`, which closes the gap where the assert's "must never be able to run containers" claim was satisfied by a host with podman installed.

Docs updated to match.

**Verification:** `ansible-lint ansible/roles/ai-dev` reports 14 fatal violations vs. 13 on the pre-change branch. The one addition is `name[casing]` on the new handler — the same violation the three existing handlers in that file already carry, so I matched the file's style rather than diverging. Every other violation is pre-existing. I could not run `ansible-playbook --syntax-check`: `group_vars/secrets.yaml` is vault-encrypted and no vault secret is available in this session. ansible-lint does parse the tasks and handlers, so the YAML and task structure are valid, but the play itself is unverified end to end, and nothing here has been run against the actual host.
